transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?
I'm here because I have an intense, overwhelming fear of dogs. It's been going on for about a year and three months now, and I finally decided I need some help with it.
I'm sorry, I didn't quite catch what you were saying. Could you please repeat your question?
Do you find yourself avoiding places or situations where you might encounter dogs due to your fear?

Yes, definitely. I completely avoid going to local parks, walking down certain streets, or even visiting friends who own pets. I will take long, exhausting detours just to make sure I don't run into one.
I'm sorry, I didn't catch that last part. Could you please repeat your question?
Can you describe what happens to you physically and emotionally when you encounter a dog or even think about encountering one?

Just thinking about running into a dog makes me incredibly anxious and uneasy. If I actually see one, I panic instantly—my heart starts pounding, I sweat, struggle to breathe, and I completely freeze in place, unable to move.
You mentioned your fear has been present for about a year and three months, but can you tell me more about what triggered it or if it seemed to develop gradually over time?
I'm not really sure how it started or whether it came on suddenly or gradually. I can't recall a specific event that triggered it, it's just been a constant struggle for over a year now.
Is your fear specifically of dogs, or does it extend to other animals or situations that might be related to dogs, such as their barking or pictures of them?
My fear is definitely centered specifically on dogs, as they are my main trigger. However, just hearing a dog bark or seeing a picture of one can also make me feel incredibly anxious.
Does your fear of dogs interfere with your daily life, relationships, or work, and have you tried any methods to cope with or overcome this fear on your own?

Yes, it severely limits my daily life and social activities because I constantly have to plan my routes and avoid outdoor spaces where dogs might be. To cope, I mostly rely on active avoidance, or I make sure to have a close friend with me as a safety net if I absolutely have to go somewhere risky.
